papers.title: Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Semantic-level Internal Reasoning Graph
papers.abstract: The Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system based on Large language model (LLM) has made significant progress. It can effectively reduce factuality hallucinations, but faithfulness hallucinations still exist. Previous methods for detecting faithfulness hallucinations either neglect to capture the models'internal reasoning processes or handle those features coarsely, making it difficult for discriminators to learn. This paper proposes a semantic-level internal reasoning graph-based method for detecting faithfulness hallucination. Specifically, we first extend the layer-wise relevance propagation algorithm from the token level to the semantic level, constructing an internal reasoning graph based on attribution vectors. This provides a more faithful semantic-level representation of dependency. Furthermore, we design a general framework based on a small pre-trained language model to utilize the dependencies in LLM's reasoning for training and hallucination detection, which can dynamically adjust the pass rate of correct samples through a threshold. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves better overall performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on RAGTruth and Dolly-15k.

papers.title: A Self-Reflective Retrieval Augmented Generation System to Eliminate Hallucination in LLM Generation
papers.abstract: In a Retrieval Augmented Generation system, the possibility of hallucination is ever prevalent, as it has been increasingly common for an AI model to produce inaccurate generations given an input, which can become increasingly more devastating for a RAG system due to its node-like generation. To solve this problem, we introduced a series of selfreflective nodes, creating a self-RAG model. To create our program, we established a series of nodes that utilized ChatGPT for generation as well as the Langchain python library and its workflow functions to piece together the nodes. A major challenge faced during the planning and development stages was the creation of the self-reflective nodes within the workflow, as these proved to be difficult to implement. To test the accuracy and capacity of this proposed Self-RAG model, multiple experiments were carried out and the result ensures a quality generation. This model should be implemented because it avoids misleading and inaccurate answers.

papers.title: LLM-powered threat intelligence: a retrieval-augmented generation approach for cyber attack investigation
papers.abstract: Threat intelligence involves collecting, analyzing, and disseminating information about cyber threats to help organizations proactively defend against attacks. However, manually investigating cyberattacks using Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) data is challenging due to its heterogeneity, complexity, and volume. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential for automating attack investigation, they suffer from hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and technical misinterpretations. To address these limitations, we propose a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based LLM system called RAGIntel, which enhances accuracy by retrieving and leveraging structured threat intelligence from MITRE ATT&CK. Our approach employs a hybrid retrieval algorithm with reranking and compression strategies to provide precise, context-aware responses. We evaluated RAGIntel on 339 attack investigation queries drawn from diverse benchmarks, using multiple evaluation metrics, and found that it delivers performance comparable to that of standalone LLMs. This study advances automated attack investigation by leveraging RAG-based LLMs, providing a scalable, accurate, and up-to-date solution for cybersecurity analysts.

papers.title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has quickly grown into a pivotal paradigm in the development of Large Language Models (LLMs). Although existing research mainly emphasizes accuracy and efficiency, the trustworthiness of RAG systems remains insufficiently explored. RAG can improve LLM reliability by grounding responses in external and up-to-date knowledge, reducing hallucinations. However, unreliable retrieval or improper knowledge utilization may still lead to undesirable outputs. To address these concerns, we propose a unified framework, Trust-RAG Compass, that assesses the trustworthiness of RAG systems across six key dimensions: factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy. Within this framework, we provide a thorough review of the existing literature along each dimension. Furthermore, we introduce an evaluation benchmark, TRC Bench (\underline{T}rust-\underline{R}AG \underline{C}ompass \underline{Bench}mark), regarding the six dimensions and conduct comprehensive evaluations for a variety of proprietary and open-source models. Our results shed light on the performance gaps between different types of LLMs across varying dimensions of trustworthiness. Finally, we identify key challenges and promising directions for future research based on our findings. Through this work, we aim to provide a structured foundation for subsequent investigations and practical guidance for developing trustworthy RAG systems in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Investigating the performance of Retrieval-Augmented Generation and fine-tuning for the development of AI-driven knowledge-based systems
papers.abstract: Generative large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the development of knowledge-based systems, enabling new possibilities in applications like ChatGPT, Bing, and Gemini. Two key strategies for domain adaptation in these systems are Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning (DFT) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In this study, we evaluate the performance of RAG and DFT on several LLM architectures, including GPT-J-6B, OPT-6.7B, LLaMA, and LLaMA-2. We use the ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR scores to evaluate the performance of the models. We also measure the performance of the models with our own designed cosine similarity-based Coverage Score (CS). Our results, based on experiments across multiple datasets, show that RAG-based systems consistently outperform those fine-tuned with DFT. Specifically, RAG models outperform DFT by an average of 17% in ROUGE, 13% in BLEU, and 36% in CS. At the same time, DFT achieves only a modest advantage in METEOR, suggesting slightly better creative capabilities. We also highlight the challenges of integrating RAG with DFT, as such integration can lead to performance degradation. Furthermore, we propose a simplified RAG-based architecture that maximizes efficiency and reduces hallucination, underscoring the advantages of RAG in building reliable, domain-adapted knowledge systems.

literature_themes.theme: Addressing Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on various methods to detect and mitigate hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). Approaches include semantic-level internal reasoning graphs for detecting faithfulness hallucinations, self-reflective nodes to enhance generation accuracy, and a comprehensive framework for assessing the trustworthiness of RAG systems across multiple dimensions. Empirical results demonstrate that RAG systems can outperform traditional fine-tuning methods in generating accurate and reliable outputs.
literature_themes.limitations: Despite advancements, challenges remain in effectively implementing self-reflective mechanisms and ensuring the trustworthiness of RAG systems. There is also a need for more robust evaluation benchmarks to assess the performance across the proposed dimensions of trustworthiness. Additionally, integrating RAG with fine-tuning strategies can lead to performance degradation.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further research into the trustworthiness and reliability of RAG systems, particularly in addressing the complexities of hallucination detection and mitigation. It identifies gaps in existing methodologies and suggests avenues for developing more trustworthy AI-driven knowledge-based systems.

literature_themes.theme: Automating Cyber Attack Investigation with LLMs
literature_themes.summary: This cluster primarily explores the use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, specifically RAGIntel, to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of cyber attack investigations by leveraging structured threat intelligence, particularly from MITRE ATT&CK. The research demonstrates that RAGIntel can provide context-aware responses to diverse attack queries, achieving performance levels comparable to standalone Large Language Models (LLMs).
literature_themes.limitations: The study acknowledges the inherent challenges of LLMs, such as hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and technical misinterpretations, which may still affect the reliability of the automated investigation process despite the improvements offered by RAGIntel.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further research into refining LLM capabilities and addressing their limitations in cybersecurity contexts, thereby supporting the identification of gaps in automated threat intelligence solutions and the potential for more robust systems.

summary: The literature on hallucination propagation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems emphasizes the need for effective detection and mitigation strategies, highlighting methods such as semantic-level internal reasoning graphs and self-reflective nodes. While RAG systems show promise in outperforming traditional fine-tuning methods, challenges remain in ensuring trustworthiness and addressing various types of hallucinations. Additionally, the application of RAG in cybersecurity contexts reveals gaps in enhancing LLM capabilities and the reliability of automated threat intelligence solutions.
scholarly_positioning: While prior research has made significant strides in addressing hallucinations within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, particularly through methods like semantic-level internal reasoning graphs and self-reflective nodes, these approaches often fall short in comprehensively tackling the diverse types of hallucinations that can arise. Existing frameworks, such as the Trust-RAG Compass, highlight the importance of trustworthiness but lack empirical solutions for enhancement. Moreover, the integration of RAG with fine-tuning strategies presents unresolved tensions that may lead to performance degradation. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing innovative methodologies for hallucination detection and mitigation, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on the reliability and trustworthiness of AI-driven knowledge systems.
research_scope: This empirical study will investigate the effectiveness of a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method for detecting and mitigating various types of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, specifically focusing on the ChatGPT model. The evaluation period will span six months, during which the model's performance will be assessed against a control group utilizing traditional fine-tuning methods. Primary outcomes will include the accuracy and reliability of generated outputs, measured through benchmark evaluations and human assessments. Secondary outcomes will focus on the trustworthiness of the RAG system, evaluated through a comprehensive framework assessing multiple dimensions of trustworthiness. The study aims to enhance the understanding of hallucination propagation and improve the robustness of AI-driven knowledge systems in diverse application domains.

technical_feasibility: The study requires access to an open-source model or hidden-state extraction capabilities from the ChatGPT model to effectively analyze internal representations. Additionally, it will need labeled datasets for benchmark evaluations and human assessments, as well as multilingual prompt sets to ensure diverse evaluation. Human participants are necessary for trustworthiness assessments, which will require ethics approval. GPU resources are essential for model training and evaluation. Annotation protocols will be needed for consistent evaluation of outputs. If only API access to the ChatGPT model is available, the research design should be adjusted to focus on output-level explanation or black-box evaluation methods instead of internal representation analysis. Missing resources include access to the model's internal states and labeled datasets, which are crucial for the proposed methodology.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated methods for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, particularly through semantic-level internal reasoning graphs; however, they treat the diversity of hallucination types as secondary, leaving unclear whether comprehensive detection strategies affect the overall trustworthiness of RAG systems. This matters theoretically because understanding the full spectrum of hallucinations can enhance the reliability of AI-driven knowledge systems; therefore, this study investigates the effectiveness of a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method for detecting various types of hallucinations within the defined scope of RAG systems.
question: How effective is a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method in detecting and mitigating various types of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems, specifically using the ChatGPT model, compared to traditional fine-tuning methods in terms of accuracy and reliability of generated outputs?
theoretical_mechanism: In this study, the independent variable is the novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method, which serves as the mediator in enhancing the detection and mitigation of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. The dependent variable is the accuracy and reliability of generated outputs, measured through various benchmarks. The theoretical framework is grounded in the interplay between technical mechanisms (such as representation features and safety detection) and user-level outcomes (such as trust and satisfaction). The causal chain posits that improved detection mechanisms lead to reduced unsafe response rates and increased refusal accuracy, ultimately enhancing user trust through perceived transparency. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of the internal reasoning graph in capturing diverse hallucination types and its direct impact on user trust metrics.
hypothesis: The implementation of a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method (independent variable) will result in a significantly higher accuracy and reliability of generated outputs (primary dependent variable) in Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems compared to traditional fine-tuning methods (comparison/control), mediated by improved detection and mitigation of various types of hallucinations.

Likely Confounds: Potential confounding variables include the inherent variability in user expectations, the influence of external factors on user trust, and the quality of the training data used for both the novel method and traditional methods.

A control group will utilize traditional fine-tuning methods for comparison. The primary outcomes will be the accuracy and reliability of generated outputs, measured through benchmark evaluations and human assessments, while secondary outcomes will focus on trustworthiness metrics. Participants will include human evaluators for trust assessments, requiring ethics approval. The study will implement ablation studies to isolate the effects of the reasoning graph on hallucination detection, and output-level explanation methods will be used to provide insights into generated outputs. phd_contribution_design: This research proposes a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method to enhance the detection and mitigation of hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, specifically targeting the ChatGPT model. The mechanism-level claim posits that this method will improve the accuracy and reliability of generated outputs by systematically addressing diverse hallucination types, a dimension often overlooked in existing literature. Current frameworks fail to comprehensively measure and validate the impact of various hallucination types on trustworthiness metrics, highlighting a significant gap in understanding. The falsifiable claim is that the implementation of this method will yield statistically significant improvements in output accuracy compared to traditional fine-tuning methods. The strongest baseline for comparison will be traditional fine-tuning approaches, while ablation studies will isolate the effects of the reasoning graph. Evidence supporting the claim will be derived from benchmark evaluations and human assessments of output quality. A negative result would suggest that the proposed method does not significantly enhance hallucination detection, challenging the theoretical framework and indicating that alternative strategies may be necessary for improving trustworthiness in RAG systems.
pre_proposal_critique: The proposed contribution design may struggle to achieve a PhD-level score due to several critical weaknesses. First, the novelty claim regarding the semantic-level internal reasoning graph lacks sufficient theoretical grounding, failing to clearly differentiate it from existing methods in hallucination detection. To address this, the proposal must articulate a robust theoretical framework that explicitly connects the new method to established theories in AI and hallucination studies. Second, the literature positioning appears shallow, as it does not adequately engage with recent advancements in RAG systems; thus, a comprehensive literature review that contextualizes the research within current debates and methodologies is essential. Lastly, the proposed metrics for evaluating accuracy and reliability may not capture the nuanced effects of hallucinations, necessitating the inclusion of more validated metrics and clear definitions for 'accuracy' and 'reliability.' Each of these objections must be addressed to strengthen the proposal's foundation and ensure its potential for significant academic contribution.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate hallucination propagation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, specifically focusing on the ChatGPT model, through the development of a novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method for detecting and mitigating diverse types of hallucinations. RAG systems are defined as AI models that integrate retrieval and generation capabilities, while hallucinations refer to outputs that are factually incorrect or nonsensical. The internal reasoning graph serves as a structured representation of a model's reasoning process. Technical feasibility assumes access to the ChatGPT model via API, labeled datasets for evaluation, and ethics approval for human assessments. The motivation stems from existing literature highlighting gaps in addressing the diversity of hallucinations and the need for comprehensive detection strategies, as prior approaches often overlook the complexities of hallucination types and their impact on trustworthiness. The research question posits: How effective is the novel semantic-level internal reasoning graph method in detecting and mitigating various types of hallucinations in RAG systems compared to traditional fine-tuning methods in terms of accuracy and reliability of generated outputs? The theoretical mechanism includes a system-level pathway where the internal reasoning graph enhances hallucination detection, leading to improved output reliability, and a user-level pathway where enhanced detection fosters user trust through perceived transparency. The falsifiable hypothesis states that the implementation of the novel method will yield significantly higher accuracy and reliability in generated outputs compared to traditional fine-tuning methods. Constructs will be operationalized using benchmark evaluations for output accuracy, human assessments for trust calibration, and detection metrics for hallucination mitigation. The methodology involves benchmark evaluations against a control group utilizing traditional fine-tuning, with ablation studies to isolate the effects of the reasoning graph. Validity will be ensured through rigorous statistical analysis, and confound control strategies will be implemented to address variability in user expectations. Theoretical novelty lies in the introduction of the semantic-level internal reasoning graph as a new construct, while technical novelty is demonstrated through the systematic approach to hallucination detection. Empirical contributions will validate the effectiveness of the proposed method through comprehensive evaluations, and practical contributions will provide guidelines for enhancing the robustness of AI-driven knowledge systems. Key limitations include potential confounding variables impacting user trust, the challenge of generalizing findings beyond the ChatGPT model, and the risk of inadequate detection of hallucinations, which will be mitigated by implementing multiple detection metrics and cross-validation with human assessments.

proposal_critique.revision_plan: Revise the gap stage to clarify the specific implications of the identified gap and strengthen its connection to existing literature. Enhance the scholarly positioning by critically comparing prior approaches and identifying unresolved tensions. Improve the clarity of the research scope by defining key terms and outcomes more precisely. Address the theoretical mechanism by explicitly stating assumptions and detailing how the proposed method mediates the relationship between hallucination detection and output reliability.

rubric_scores.level: 9-11: understandable but partially broad or insufficiently operationalized
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal identifies hallucination propagation in RAG systems as a research problem but lacks precise operational definitions for key concepts like 'hallucination' and 'trustworthiness'. The research question is somewhat clear but could benefit from more specificity regarding the types of hallucinations being addressed. Major weaknesses: Vague definitions of constructs and insufficient operationalization of key concepts hinder clarity. The motivation is present but not strongly articulated. Next band requirements: To move into the next band, the proposal must provide clearer definitions of key concepts and a more focused research question that delineates the specific types of hallucinations being investigated.

rubric_scores.level: 12-13: mostly coherent with minor reasoning gaps
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal demonstrates a logical flow from problem identification to hypothesis formulation, but some assumptions regarding the effectiveness of the internal reasoning graph are not fully justified. The causal claims are present but require stronger empirical backing. Major weaknesses: Insufficient justification for the assumptions about the internal reasoning graph's effectiveness in improving detection and mitigation of hallucinations. Next band requirements: Strengthening the empirical justification for assumptions and ensuring that all causal claims are explicitly supported by existing literature would enhance coherence.

The proposal introduces a novel method (semantic-level internal reasoning graph) but does not sufficiently differentiate it from existing methods in hallucination detection. While it aims to fill a gap, the novelty claims are not robustly supported by theoretical grounding. Major weaknesses: Lack of a clear theoretical framework connecting the new method to existing literature limits the perceived originality and contribution. Next band requirements: A more explicit articulation of how the proposed method differs from existing approaches and its theoretical implications would strengthen the novelty claims.

The methodology is generally sound, with plans for benchmark evaluations and ablation studies. However, the reliance on access to the ChatGPT model and labeled datasets raises concerns about feasibility. Major weaknesses: Potential limitations in accessing necessary resources and the lack of detailed plans for addressing these limitations could impact the study's feasibility. Next band requirements: Providing contingency plans for resource access issues and more detailed descriptions of evaluation metrics would improve methodological rigor.

rubric_scores.level: 9-11: relevant literature used but somewhat surface-level
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal references relevant literature but lacks depth in synthesizing existing work and identifying specific gaps. The positioning relative to current research is not sufficiently critical. Major weaknesses: Shallow engagement with the literature and insufficient identification of unresolved tensions or contradictions limit scholarly positioning. Next band requirements: A more comprehensive literature review that critically engages with existing methodologies and identifies specific gaps would enhance scholarly positioning.

rubric_scores.level: 5-6: strong master-level but limited theoretical depth
rubric_scores.justification: The proposal demonstrates some theoretical sophistication but lacks depth in discussing the mechanisms underlying the proposed method and its implications for the field. Major weaknesses: Limited discussion of the broader implications of the research and insufficient exploration of potential limitations and failure modes. Next band requirements: Incorporating a more thorough discussion of theoretical mechanisms and broader implications would enhance academic depth.

The proposal is generally well-structured and clear, but some terminology is imprecise, and there are areas where conciseness could be improved. Major weaknesses: Some sections are repetitive or could be more concise, affecting overall readability. Next band requirements: Improving precision in terminology and enhancing conciseness would strengthen the overall presentation.

evaluation.comments: Total score: 69.0/100. Academic level: Master's-level. Major strengths: Identifies a relevant and timely research problem in AI safety.; Proposes a novel methodological approach to hallucination detection. Major weaknesses: Lacks clear operational definitions of key concepts.; Insufficient theoretical grounding for novelty claims.; Limited engagement with existing literature. Required improvements for true PhD-level quality: Enhance clarity and specificity in defining key constructs.; Strengthen theoretical framing and empirical justification for claims.; Engage more deeply with existing literature to identify gaps. Final verdict: The proposal demonstrates potential but lacks the depth and rigor expected of PhD-level research. Significant improvements are needed to meet the standards of originality, methodological rigor, and theoretical contribution.
